endorsements.quote: All AI healthcare models used in children should be tested for fairness using an appropriate definition of fairness and a suitable metric of fairness that caters to the specific context.

Datasets should include a diversity of children’s data, including children from different regions, ages, socioeconomic conditions, and ethnicities, in order to remove prejudicial bias against children or against certain groups of children that results in discrimination and exclusion13.
If needed, pre-processing, in-processing, and/or post-processing can be implemented to mitigate bias.
A balance must be found such that there is sufficient data about children for the development of AI systems while minimizing data collection to safeguard privacy and security65.

UNICEF promotes children maintaining control over their own data with the capacity to access, securely share, understand the use of, and delete their data, in accordance with their age and maturity65.
UNICEF advocates continuously assessing and monitoring AI’s impact on children throughout the entire AI development life cycle and testing AI systems for safety, security, and robustness13.

Moreover, AI models must be also continuously updated and retrained to account for new pediatric data7, reflecting such changes to ensure that the outputs from the models remain accurate, reproducible, and relevant.
AI-enabled systems must have cybersecurity measures in place to protect against unauthorized access, modification and disruption, whilst maintaining confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Medical professionals should be informed about the use of an AI-enabled device and the limitations of the AI system including inclusion and exclusion criteria.

Parents and children who interact with an AI medical system also have the right to be informed using age-appropriate language and an inclusive manner, to understand how the system works and how it uses and maintains confidential data13.
Unlike adults, who are able to consent, a parent or legal guardian must provide consent for the collection of a child’s medical data or the use of an AI-enabled device in a child.

As children mature and attain the age of consent, they can reverse the consent previously provided by their parent or legal guardian and exercise their ‘right to be forgotten’ and for their data to be erased74.

Physicians should determine prior to the use of any AI system whether the device has been specifically evaluated in pediatric patients by referring to the indications for use section and the 510(k) summary in the FDA 510(k) database12.
Mechanisms to involve a broad spectrum of stakeholders, including the children themselves, parents, clinicians, and developers, in the design and evaluation processes.
For medical-legal purposes, the audit trail for AI in pediatric patients may need to be retained until the age of maturity (18 years) plus an additional 3 years (21 years)7.
Ethical Risk Assessment: A structured evaluation of potential risks to children’s well-being posed by AI models, including bias, discrimination, and unintended outcomes.
Developers must clearly document when AI models are created, revalidated, and set to expire7.

Before an AI system is implemented for child health, there must exist convincing evidence that it results in no harm or that benefits can be confidently expected to outweigh harm, notwithstanding any benefits that it can bring to the children.

unlisted_practices: Developers should use interpretable rather than black-box AI for children, especially for irreversible decisions.
Include children in AI development data and trials, and ensure meaningful child participation in design.
Provide accessible mechanisms for reporting and escalating concerns about AI to clinicians and families, and offer redress in case of harm.
Design AI for children with safety-by-design, privacy-by-design and inclusion-by-design.
Obtain assent from children and consent from decisionally competent adolescents in addition to parents, and revisit consent periodically as the child grows.
Disclose to parents and competent children when an AI device has not been evaluated in children, and exercise caution and clinical judgment.
Provide child safety tools controlling content exposure, profile visibility, contact, and location sharing for children and parents.
Fail-safe design and robustness testing of AI systems for children.
Equip policymakers, management and developers with knowledge of AI and children's rights.
Establish AI regulatory bodies to monitor and correct infringements of children's rights, and regularly review governance frameworks.
Governments and businesses should invest in infrastructure to address the digital divide and fund research on AI for children.
Disclose conflicts of interest between AI app developers and manufacturers of recommended products to patients and parents.
Include a pediatric use statement and label-style summary on AI device documentation.
